benefits: Promotes relaxation
Improves posture
Enhances concentration

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Spine vertical, hips externally rotated, feet resting on opposite thighs

cues: Stack the crown of the head directly over the sitting bones.
Let the knees soften toward the floor without forcing.
Rest the backs of the hands on the knees, palms open.
Breathe into the lower belly to anchor the pose.
modifications: Use a folded blanket under the hips to elevate the pelvis.
Practice Half-Lotus or easy cross-legged if full Lotus is unavailable.
Sit against a wall for back support during extended meditation.
history: The defining posture of ancient yoga tradition, described by Patanjali as the ideal meditation seat. Appears in nearly every yogic text thereafter.

benefits: Improves spinal flexibility
Stimulates digestion
Relieves tension in the back and shoulders

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Axial rotation of the spine, pelvis grounded

cues: Ground both sitting bones evenly before rotating.
Lengthen through the crown on the inhale, rotate on the exhale.
Keep the lower belly gently engaged throughout.
Use the front arm against the knee as a gentle lever, not a force.
modifications: Extend the bottom leg straight for a gentler hip position.
Sit on a folded blanket to elevate the hips.
Use a strap around the top knee for a lighter twist.
history: Named for the sage Matsyendra, described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika as one of the 84 classical asanas essential for awakening Kundalini energy.

benefits: Strengthens legs and core
Improves balance and stability
Opens hips and chest

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Front knee at 90-degree angle, arms extended parallel to the floor, torso centered

cues: Front knee tracks directly over the second toe — don't let it collapse inward.
Keep the torso stacked vertically, not leaning forward or back.
Reach through both fingertips as if pulling the arms apart.
Root the back foot edge firmly; outer hip drives back.
modifications: Shorten the stance to reduce knee load.
Place hands on hips if shoulders are fatigued.
Use a chair alongside for balance support.
history: A modern posture codified by Krishnamacharya in the early 20th century, influenced by Indian wrestling stances and European gymnastics.

benefits: Accessible meditation seat for all levels
Grounds and calms the nervous system
Gently opens the hips over time

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Spine erect, shins crossed, hands resting on knees, crown of head lifting

cues: Feel both sitting bones equally heavy on the ground.
Gently draw the lower belly in to support the lumbar spine.
Let the shoulders release away from the ears.
Soften the jaw and the space between the eyebrows.
modifications: Sit on a block or folded blanket to tilt the pelvis forward.
Cross ankles instead of shins for less hip demand.
Lean against a wall to maintain an upright spine.
history: One of the oldest documented asanas, used across all major ancient traditions as the default posture for pranayama and meditation.

benefits: Promotes meditative stillness
Activates the root energy center (Muladhara Chakra)
Encourages sustained, upright spinal posture

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: One heel pressed to perineum, second heel stacked above, spine elongated

cues: Place the lower heel at the perineum before settling the upper heel.
Allow both knees to descend toward the earth without forcing.
Maintain length through the spine from sacrum to crown.
Use the breath to deepen stillness, not muscle effort.
modifications: Use Sukhasana if Siddhasana creates knee discomfort.
Elevate hips on a firm bolster or meditation cushion.
Alternate which leg is on top in each session.
history: Revered in Tantric traditions as the second most important seat after Padmasana, said to activate the Muladhara Chakra through heel pressure at the perineum.

benefits: Strengthens the muscles of the back and spine
Stimulates abdominal organs and digestion
Opens the chest and supports respiratory function

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Pelvis grounded, elbows soft, chest lifted, shoulder blades drawing together and down

cues: Keep the pelvis and tops of the feet rooted to the mat.
Micro-bend the elbows — this is a back-bend, not a push-up.
Draw the shoulder blades toward each other and down.
Gaze forward or slightly upward; never strain the neck back.
modifications: Lift only a few inches — baby cobra is fully valid.
Place a rolled blanket under the lower belly for support.
Use Sphinx pose (forearms down) as a gentler preparation.
history: Documented in the Gheranda Samhita (17th c.), described as awakening the Kundalini and increasing digestive fire.

benefits: Stimulates the thyroid and parathyroid glands
Reverses gravitational effect on lymph and venous circulation
Calms the nervous system and supports sleep

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Weight on shoulders and upper arms, spine vertical, legs extended overhead, chin to chest

cues: Bear weight on the upper arms and shoulders — never the neck.
Bring the chin lightly toward the chest (Jalandhara Bandha).
Stack hips over shoulders and feet over hips.
Keep the elbows close together; hands support the mid-back.
modifications: Use a folded blanket under the shoulders to protect the cervical spine.
Legs-up-the-wall (Viparita Karani) is a safe, supported alternative.
Bend the knees to reduce load while building shoulder strength.
history: Called the 'mother of asanas' in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. Considered a master restorative and endocrine-regulating posture.

benefits: Increases cerebral circulation
Builds deep core and shoulder stability
Cultivates focus and mental clarity

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Forearms grounded in triangle, crown of head lightly contacting mat, shoulders stacked above elbows, legs fully extended

cues: Forearms form a triangle base — not too wide, not too narrow.
Press through the forearms: 90% of weight there, 10% on head.
Stack shoulders directly above elbows before lifting.
Engage the core fully before attempting to raise the legs.
modifications: Practice the base (dolphin pose) to build shoulder strength first.
Use a wall for support while developing balance.
Half-headstand with knees bent is a safe intermediate step.
history: Known as the 'king of asanas' in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. Practiced daily by Iyengar himself for decades; described in his Light on Yoga.

benefits: Stretches the entire anterior body
Strengthens the posterior chain
Massages abdominal organs, supporting digestive health

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Pelvis grounded, ankles held by hands, knees hip-width, chest and thighs lifting away from the mat

cues: Kick the feet back into the hands to create the lift passively.
Keep the knees no wider than hip-width throughout.
Breathe into the chest — the belly compression limits breath there.
Gaze forward or slightly up; protect the neck.
modifications: Lift one leg at a time (half bow) if full bow is inaccessible.
Use a strap around the ankles to close the gap.
Place a blanket under the hip bones for cushioning.
history: Cataloged in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. The name means 'bow' — the body forms the arc of a strung bow, the arms as the string.

benefits: Deeply stretches the cervical and thoracic spine
Stimulates the abdominal organs and thyroid
Quiets the mind and encourages introspection

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Shoulders grounded, feet resting on the floor behind the head, spine elongated, hands supporting the lower back or interlaced on the mat

cues: Transition from Shoulderstand: lower both legs together toward the floor.
Press the tops of the shoulders into the mat to protect the neck.
Walk the toes further back to lengthen the spine.
Interlace fingers on the mat or keep hands supporting the back.
modifications: Rest feet on a chair instead of the floor.
Use a wall behind you so feet touch it without full extension.
Skip this pose entirely if there is any neck injury.
history: Described in the Gheranda Samhita as 'destroyer of diseases.' The name means plow, referencing the body's resemblance to an agricultural plow.

benefits: Builds exceptional wrist, forearm, and core strength
Stimulates the digestive fire (Agni)
Develops full-body muscular integration and balance

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Elbows pressed into the abdomen, body parallel to the floor, legs extended, gaze forward

cues: Plant the elbows firmly into the soft abdomen just below the navel.
Keep elbows together — this is the fulcrum of the entire balance.
Shift weight slowly forward until the feet lighten off the mat.
Gaze slightly forward; body forms one straight plank.
modifications: Practice crow pose (Bakasana) first to build wrist and core strength.
Use a block under the forehead for graduated weight shift.
Try one leg at a time before attempting the full posture.
history: One of the most difficult medieval asanas described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. Said to stimulate digestive fire and cure diseases of the stomach.

benefits: Deeply opens the hips and outer glutes
Stretches the shoulders and triceps
Supports healthy hip and shoulder joint mobility

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Knees stacked at midline, one arm reaching up and bending back, opposite arm reaching down and bending up to clasp

cues: Stack the knees directly on top of each other at the midline.
Lengthen the upper elbow toward the ceiling before bending.
If hands don't meet, use a strap between them.
Keep both sitting bones even — one side will want to lift.
modifications: Sit in Dandasana with legs extended if knee stacking is uncomfortable.
Use a strap for the arm bind.
Practice the arm work independently while seated in a chair.
history: Described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. The name means 'cow face' — the stacked legs resemble a cow's face in certain traditional depictions.

benefits: Lengthens the entire posterior chain from heels to head
Calms the nervous system and reduces anxiety
Stimulates the kidneys, liver, and digestive organs

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Legs extended, spine lengthening forward, pelvis tilting anteriorly, hinging from the hips rather than rounding the back

cues: Hinge from the hip sockets, not the lower back.
Lead with the chest — lengthen the front body first.
Flex the feet gently to engage the hamstrings from the ankle.
Use an exhale to deepen; never force the fold.
modifications: Use a strap around the feet to maintain a long spine.
Micro-bend the knees to take strain off the hamstrings.
Sit on a blanket to tilt the pelvis forward more easily.
history: One of the most prescribed poses in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, said to awaken the Kundalini and kindle the digestive fire.

benefits: Aids digestion when practiced after meals
Strengthens the pelvic floor
Provides a stable, grounded seat for pranayama

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Kneeling with shins on the mat, sitting bones resting on heels, spine vertical, hands on thighs

cues: Rest sitting bones fully onto heels; big toes may touch.
Stack the spine directly above the pelvis.
Rest palms face-down on the thighs, shoulders relaxed.
Breathe slowly — this is ideal for post-meal digestion.
modifications: Place a folded blanket between calves and thighs to reduce knee compression.
Use a rolled blanket under the ankles if dorsiflexion is limited.
Sit in a chair and practice the upright spine alignment instead.
history: Described in the Gheranda Samhita as a destroyer of fatigue. The only asana recommended by Ayurveda and yoga texts for use immediately after eating.

benefits: Integrates the physical and energetic effects of practice
Activates the parasympathetic nervous system
Reduces stress, blood pressure, and mental fatigue

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Full body supine, arms slightly away from the torso, palms facing up, legs hip-width apart and fully relaxed

cues: Let the feet fall open naturally to the sides.
Move the arms a few inches from the body, palms sky-facing.
Release all muscular effort — allow the floor to fully support you.
Stay for a minimum of 5 minutes to allow full nervous system integration.
modifications: Place a bolster under the knees to release the lower back.
Use an eye pillow to deepen the sense of withdrawal.
Cover with a blanket if the room is cool — body temperature drops.
history: Described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika as the remover of fatigue and the posture that brings the mind to rest. Now understood to activate the parasympathetic nervous system.

benefits: Strengthens the legs, glutes, and core
Opens the hip flexors of the back leg
Builds focus, determination, and postural awareness

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Front knee stacked over ankle at 90 degrees, back foot grounded at 45 degrees, hips squared forward, arms raised overhead

cues: Ground the outer edge of the back foot, angled 45 degrees.
Square the hips forward — front hip back, back hip forward.
Bend the front knee to 90 degrees, stacked over the ankle.
Lift through the arms without shrugging the shoulders.
modifications: Shorten the stance to ease the hip square.
Use hands on hips if the shoulder lift is fatiguing.
Practice against a wall to cue the hip square.
history: Named for the mythological warrior Virabhadra. Codified by Krishnamacharya in the 20th century, though the narrative origin traces to ancient Shaiva texts.

benefits: Lengthens the lateral chain and inner thigh
Strengthens the legs and stabilizes the knee
Improves balance and spatial awareness

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Legs wide, front foot turned out 90 degrees, torso extending laterally, bottom hand to shin or block, top arm reaching vertically

cues: Front foot turns out 90 degrees, back foot 15–30 degrees in.
Extend the torso laterally over the front leg before descending the hand.
Stack the top shoulder directly above the bottom shoulder.
Turn the gaze up toward the top hand, or keep it forward to protect the neck.
modifications: Place the bottom hand on a block to reduce lateral reach.
Keep a micro-bend in the front knee to protect the joint.
Practice against a wall to maintain the flat-plane alignment.
history: Extensively described and photographed by B.K.S. Iyengar in Light on Yoga (1966). One of the most studied standing poses in modern yoga biomechanics.

benefits: Lengthens the posterior chain and shoulders
Builds upper-body and core strength
Functions as a restorative transition and mild inversion

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Hips lifted toward ceiling, heels pressing toward the floor, spine elongated, weight evenly distributed through hands and feet

cues: Press evenly through all four corners of each palm.
Internally rotate the upper arms to widen the shoulder blades.
Reach the sitting bones toward the ceiling — that is the apex.
Soften the knees if needed; a long spine matters more than straight legs.
modifications: Bend both knees generously to protect the lower back.
Hands on blocks reduce wrist load.
Puppy pose (knees down, hips over knees) as a gentler alternative.
history: Popularized globally by Krishnamacharya's lineage. Described extensively by Iyengar in Light on Yoga as both a forward bend and mild inversion.

benefits: Establishes postural awareness and neutral alignment
Activates the feet, legs, and core for stable grounding
Serves as the foundation from which all standing poses arise

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Feet together or hip-width, weight evenly distributed, legs engaged, spine neutral, arms at sides, crown of head lifting

cues: Distribute weight evenly across all four corners of both feet.
Engage the thighs gently without locking the knees.
Lengthen the tailbone down while the crown lifts up.
Arms hang freely at the sides, palms lightly facing forward.
modifications: Stand with feet hip-width apart for more stability.
Stand with back against a wall to feel neutral spinal alignment.
Slightly bend the knees if standing fully straight causes lower back strain.
history: The foundational standing pose of the Iyengar system, described in Light on Yoga as the basis from which all standing poses derive their architecture.

benefits: Develops single-leg balance and proprioception
Strengthens the ankle, knee, and hip stabilizers
Cultivates mental focus and nervous system coordination

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Standing leg straight and engaged, sole of foot on inner thigh or calf (never the knee), hips level, hands at heart or overhead

cues: Root through all four corners of the standing foot.
Place the raised foot on the inner thigh or calf — never the knee joint.
Keep both hips level; do not let the hip of the raised leg hike.
Fix the gaze (Drishti) on a still point to stabilize the balance.
modifications: Keep the toes of the raised foot touching the floor as a kickstand.
Use a wall or chair lightly for balance support.
Bring hands to heart center rather than overhead.
history: Described by Iyengar in Light on Yoga. One of the first balance poses introduced to beginners in the modern Hatha tradition.

benefits: Strengthens the quadriceps, glutes, and lower back
Builds heat and energizes the body
Improves ankle and thoracic mobility under load

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Feet together, knees bent as if sitting in a chair, torso angled forward, arms raised alongside ears

cues: Feet together or hip-width; weight shifts into the heels.
Bend the knees deeply — aim for thighs approaching parallel to the floor.
Torso tilts forward at roughly 45 degrees to counter the weight.
Reach the arms alongside the ears; shoulders stay away from the ears.
modifications: Take feet hip-width apart for more stability.
Hands on thighs or at heart center to reduce shoulder fatigue.
Use a wall at the back for support to build quadriceps strength.
history: Widely used in Ashtanga sequences as a powerful heat-building pose. Described in Iyengar's Light on Yoga as both a challenge and a toner for the entire body.

benefits: Strengthens the posterior chain including glutes and hamstrings
Opens the chest and hip flexors
Supports thyroid function and calms the nervous system

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Feet flat on the mat hip-width apart, hips lifted, arms extended alongside the body or clasped beneath the spine, knees tracking over ankles

cues: Feet are hip-width apart, toes pointing straight forward.
Press through the feet to lift the hips; squeeze the glutes gently at the top.
Roll the shoulders under to clasp the hands beneath the back.
Knees stay over ankles — prevent the feet from splaying.
modifications: Place a block under the sacrum for a supported, restorative version.
Keep arms alongside body (don't clasp) if shoulders are tight.
Do single-leg variation to reduce lower back load.
history: Thoroughly documented by Iyengar in Light on Yoga (1966) as both a back strengthener and mild inversion with thyroid benefits.

benefits: Gently decompresses the lumbar spine
Provides a safe resting position between active poses
Calms the nervous system and supports parasympathetic recovery

visualizer_data.primary_alignment: Hips toward heels, forehead to the mat, arms extended forward or resting alongside the body

cues: Bring the big toes together and let the knees widen to the edges of the mat.
Sink the hips toward the heels with each exhale.
Extend the arms forward fully or let them rest alongside the body.
Rest the forehead on the mat — the contact point itself calms the nervous system.
modifications: Place a bolster under the chest for a fully supported version.
Fold a blanket between thighs and calves if hips don't reach heels.
Use a block under the forehead for a more restful neck position.
history: Developed within the 20th-century postural yoga tradition as a standardized resting posture between more demanding poses.
